newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore says his China trip will lead to progress.
newsitem.headline: Gore says his China trip will lead to progress.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Thursday predicted his two days of talks with Chinese leaders would lead to "significant progress" within the next few months on several issues now dividing Washington and Beijing.

"This mission here this week is part of President Clinton's efforts to establish a high-level dialogue that will enable our two nations to build a new era of cooperation for a new century," he told the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai.
"We have had full and vigorous discussions, very productive discussions and I'm optimistic that in the coming months we will make significant progress on many of these issues," he added.
Gore did not specify what areas would see progress.

The most senior U.S. official to visit China since the crackdown on student demonstrations in Beijing in 1989, Gore's discussions with Chinese leaders covered a wide range of tricky topics including human rights, trade disputes and Taiwan.
He also raised reports that China tried to make donations to the re-election campaigns of some U.S. politicians last year.
China has vigorously denied the charges.

In his meeting with Gore on Wednesday, Chinese President Jiang Zemin warned the United States not to interfere over Taiwan, hinting that the sensitive issue still had the potential to undermine a Sino-U.S. rapprochement.
But Jiang said that differences on individual issues should not impair overall ties.

"In the history of the development of Sino-U.S. relations, the (Taiwan) issue has experienced repeated hindrances, which even undermined the process of improving and developing Sino-U.S. relations," official media quoted Jiang as saying.

Relations chilled in March last year when Washington sent two aircraft groups to seas near Taiwan to monitor missile tests and wargames held by Beijing in a bid to intimidate rival Taipei before the island's first direct presidential elections.
China has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since the two were split at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949 and has vowed to take the island by force if it declares independence.
Gore's visit was aimed at healing the damage to ties caused by the Taiwan row and making progress on other areas of disagreement.
At the end of the talks on Wednesday, Gore said he saw the prospects for the improvement of relations between the two powers as bright.
Earlier on Thursday, Gore went to China's ancient capital of Xian and inspected the more than 2000-year-old army of terracotta warrior statues erected to fend off outside invaders.
In a relaxed and playful mood, Gore inspected the excavation site, where 7,000 life-sized figures of warriors once stood guard for China's first emperor, Qin Shihuang.
"How can you tell Al Gore from a tomb full of terracotta warriors?" a handful of reporters were asked by Gore, who has a legendary reputation for being formal and proper in public.
"He's the stiff one," Gore said with a broad smile as he walked past a formation of motionless statues made of fired clay.

On Friday, Gore was to fly to South Korea for talks with President Kim Young-sam and a visit to U.S. troops stationed along the Demilitarized Zone that separates the two Koreas. He is due to return to Washington late on Saturday.
